summary: ‘To have’ is the verb 有 yǒu: 我有一个哥哥 ‘I have an elder brother’. 有 never changes — the same for every person and every time — and with a place first it means ‘there is / there are’: 这里有很多人 ‘there are many people here’. Its negation is irregular, 没有 (S08), never *不有.

blocks.caption: 我 + 有 + 两个 + 弟弟

items.title: 有 — having (owner first)
points: 我有三本书 ‘I have three books’
她有一个女儿 ‘she has a daughter’

items.title: 有 — there is (place first)
points: 这里有很多人 ‘there are many people here’
我家有四口人 ‘my family has four people’

items.title: 在 — is at (the known thing first)
points: 书在这里 ‘the book is here’
我妈妈在那里 ‘my mother is over there’

blocks.title: One verb for ‘have’ and ‘there is’
blocks.text: 有 means ‘have’ when an owner comes first (我有两个弟弟) and ‘there is’ when a place comes first (这里有很多人) — one verb, read from what stands before it.

blocks.title: Counting a family
blocks.text: 我家有四口人 ‘there are four of us in my family’ — family members are counted with the measure word 口 ‘mouth’.

blocks.title: No 不 with 有
blocks.text: 有 is the one verb that is negated only with 没: 我没有哥哥 (S08), never *我不有.

askYourself: Who has it? → owner first, then 有.
One thing or a number of things? → number + measure word + noun after 有: 我有两个弟弟.
Is it what exists at a place? → place first: 这里有… ‘there is … here’.
Is it where a known thing is? → thing + 在 + place (书在这里), not 有.
Do I need ‘not have’? → 没有 (S08), never 不有.
steps: what is had — with number and measure word if counted

traps: *我是有一个哥哥 → 我有一个哥哥 (no 是).
*这里是很多人 → 这里有很多人 (existence uses 有).

quiz.why: 有 for ‘have’; 两 before a measure word.

quiz.q: ‘The book is here.’ (a book we know)
The form of 有 after 他们?
quiz.why: 有 never changes for the person.
Family members are counted with 口.

notes.text: Greek έχω ‘have’ conjugates (έχω, έχεις, έχει), and ‘there is’ is υπάρχει (in speech also έχει: έχει ψωμί;). Chinese 有 does both and never changes: 我有面包, 这里有面包. Negation: δεν έχω ~ 没有, never *不有.

Russian у меня есть ‘at me there is’ uses one word, есть, for ‘have’ and ‘there is’ (Здесь есть кафе) — so does Chinese 有. нет (у меня нет …) ~ 没有: both negate ‘have’ and ‘there is’ with a special form.
Spanish has tener ‘have’ and hay ‘there is’; Chinese uses 有 for both: tengo dos hermanos ~ 我有两个哥哥, hay mucha gente ~ 这里有很多人.
English has two constructions, ‘I have’ and ‘there is’; Chinese has one verb, 有, with the owner or the place first: 我有书 / 桌子上有书. ‘There is’ never uses 是: *这里是很多人.
French il y a ‘there is’ already uses avoir ‘have’; Chinese goes all the way: 有 is ‘have’ and ‘there is’ (j’ai un frère ~ 我有一个哥哥, il y a beaucoup de monde ~ 这里有很多人).
German haben and es gibt are two constructions; Chinese 有 covers both: ich habe ein Buch ~ 我有一本书, hier gibt es viele Leute ~ 这里有很多人.
Hindi says ‘near me is a car’ (मेरे पास कार है) and ‘my two brothers are’ (मेरे दो भाई हैं); Chinese uses one verb with the owner as subject: 我有一辆车, 我有两个哥哥.
Persian dāshtan ‘have’ (dāram, dāri) ~ 有, but conjugated; ‘there is’ is hast. Chinese uses 有 for both and never changes it.
Marathi says ‘with me is a book’ (माझ्याकडे पुस्तक आहे) and ‘to me is a brother’ (मला एक भाऊ आहे); Chinese makes the owner the subject of 有: 我有一本书, 我有一个哥哥.
Arabic has no verb ‘have’: ʿindī kitāb ‘at me (is) a book’, and hunāka for ‘there is’. Chinese uses the verb 有 for both, with the owner as subject: 我有一本书.

Hebrew yesh li ‘there is to me’ uses yesh for ‘have’ and ‘there is’ and ein for both negatives — just like 有 / 没有. The difference: Chinese makes the owner the subject (我有), Hebrew puts him after le- (li).
Turkish var / yok cover ‘there is’ and ‘have’ (kardeşim var ‘I have a brother’, burada çay var ‘there is tea here’) — Chinese 有 / 没有 work the same way, but the owner is a plain subject: 我有一个哥哥.
Japanese ある / いる mean ‘there is’ and also ‘have’ (車がある ‘I have a car’), split by animacy (いる for people and animals). Chinese 有 serves for everything, living or not.
Korean 있다 is ‘there is’, ‘have’ and also ‘be at’ (학교에 있어요 ‘is at school’); Chinese splits it: 有 for ‘have / there is’, 在 for ‘be at’ (他在学校).
Finnish says ‘at me is a car’ (minulla on auto); Chinese says ‘I have a car’, with the owner as subject: 我有一辆车.
Hungarian says ‘to me is my car’ (nekem van autóm) and has a special negative, nincs; Chinese has a plain verb ‘have’, 有, and a special negative, 没有.
Swahili ‘have’ is ‘be with’: nina gari ‘I have a car’, sina ‘I don’t have’; ‘there is’ is kuna. Chinese uses one verb for both, 有, and one negative, 没有.
Luganda ‘have’ is ‘be with’ (nnina ‘I have’), with the person prefix; Chinese has one unchanging verb, 有.
Vietnamese có is ‘have’ and ‘there is’, exactly like 有: tôi có hai anh trai ~ 我有两个哥哥, ở đây có nhiều người ~ 这里有很多人.
Inuktitut expresses ‘have’ with a suffix on the noun, inside one verb word (‘brother-have-I’). Chinese keeps separate words: 我 + 有 + 一个哥哥.

seeAlso.note: German haben is conjugated (ich habe, du hast, er hat) and takes the accusative; Chinese 有 never changes.
Arabic has no verb ‘to have’: عِنْدِي ‘at me’ or لِي ‘to me’ + the thing; Chinese 有 is a real verb, but it also means ‘there is’.
Hebrew says יֵשׁ לִי ‘there is to me’ — like Chinese 有, one word serves for ‘there is’ and ‘have’.
